opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to a few things, and the first one is really about control. When AI starts making or heavily shaping business decisions, whether that's pricing, supply chain planning, customer service, or credit risk, it stops being just a tool you rent and becomes part of how the company actually thinks. If that core decision-making layer sits entirely inside someone else's black box, you're exposed. You don't fully understand why a decision was made, you can't easily audit it, and you can't adjust it quickly when your business changes.

The second piece is data. Every company has its own proprietary data: its customers, its operations, its history of what worked and what didn't. That data is often the real moat. General-purpose models are incredibly capable, but they don't know your business. The companies that get the most value are the ones that can combine strong foundation models with their own data, through fine-tuning, retrieval, or building evaluation systems around their own use cases. And to do that well, you need some in-house capability. Not necessarily training models from scratch, but at least knowing how to adapt, deploy, and measure them.

Third, there's cost and efficiency. At small scale, calling an API is the obvious choice. But once AI is embedded in thousands or millions of decisions a day, inference cost becomes a real line item. Having the expertise to pick the right model size, optimize serving, maybe run open-source models on your own infrastructure, that can make a big difference to the economics.

And finally there's privacy, compliance, and trust. In regulated industries especially, you may simply not be allowed to send certain data outside, and you need to be able to explain decisions to regulators and customers.

That said, I don't think "build your own" means every company should become an AI research lab. That's usually not wise. What I see working best is a layered approach: rely on the best available foundation models and infrastructure, but build internal muscle around data, evaluation, integration, and the application layer, the parts that are truly specific to your business. That's where differentiation comes from, and that's the part you don't want to outsource completely.

r001.rationale: The response says relying entirely on another party’s AI black box leaves a company exposed and limits its ability to understand, audit, or adjust decisions.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the simplest way to put it is this: when AI was mostly a productivity tool — helping you write an email faster, summarize a document — it didn't really matter whose model you used. You could treat it like a utility. But the moment AI starts touching actual business decisions — how you price, which customers you prioritize, how you allocate inventory, what you flag as risk — the model stops being a utility and becomes part of your core logic. And nobody wants their core logic to be a black box they rent from someone else.

There are a few concrete reasons behind that. The first is data. The decisions that matter in a business are driven by proprietary data — your transaction history, your customer behavior, your operational quirks. A general-purpose model doesn't know any of that, and more importantly, the value you can extract from that data is exactly the thing you don't want to hand to a vendor who serves your competitors too. So owning the capability to train, fine-tune, or at least deeply customize models on your own data becomes a competitive moat, not just an engineering preference.

The second is control and accountability. If a model makes a decision that costs you money or creates a compliance problem, you need to be able to explain what happened, reproduce it, and fix it. That's very hard when the model changes underneath you every few months and you have no visibility into it. Companies that have lived through a vendor deprecating an API they depended on learn this lesson quickly.

The third is economics. At small scale, calling an API is obviously cheaper than building anything. But once AI is in the critical path and you're running millions of inferences a day, the unit economics flip. At that point, having your own infrastructure, your own optimized models, maybe open-source models you've adapted, often ends up being both cheaper and faster.

Now, I want to be careful here — "build your own" doesn't mean every company should train a frontier model from scratch. That would be absurd. What it means is having the in-house capability to understand, adapt, deploy, and evaluate models, and the infrastructure to do it reliably. The open-source ecosystem has made this far more accessible than it was even two years ago. You can stand on top of very strong open models and add the layer that's specific to you.

So I'd frame it less as "build versus buy" and more as: as AI becomes decision-making rather than assistance, the part that's specific to your business is the part you have to own. The question each company should ask is where that line falls for them.

r001.rationale: The response says business decision models become part of a company's core logic and that companies do not want this logic to be a black box rented from someone else.

astra-6.text:
I think a big reason is that, as AI moves from helping people find information to making business decisions, it becomes part of a company’s core capability. You want it to understand your customers, your internal processes, and the trade-offs that matter to your business. A general-purpose model doesn’t automatically have that context.

There’s also a question of control. If AI is influencing pricing or how you allocate resources, you need to be able to evaluate its decisions and improve it when something goes wrong. That requires internal expertise, even if the underlying model comes from someone else.

So building your own AI capabilities doesn’t necessarily mean training a foundation model from scratch. It could mean building the data infrastructure, the evaluation process, and the integration into your workflows. The important thing is owning the ability to turn AI into something that works for your particular business.

r001.rationale: The response says companies need internal expertise to evaluate and improve AI decisions, even when the underlying model comes from someone else, which conveys avoiding complete reliance on an external system.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that AI is becoming part of how a company makes decisions, rather than just a tool that helps employees work faster. Those decisions depend on your own data, your workflows, and the knowledge you’ve accumulated about your customers. So companies have a reason to build capabilities that reflect those things.

That doesn’t necessarily mean training a foundation model from scratch. You can use models from other providers. But you still want the ability to connect them to your business, evaluate whether they’re making good decisions, and improve them when they’re not. As you delegate more decisions to AI, that ability becomes a core competency.

r001.rationale: The response says companies can use outside models while retaining the ability to connect them to their business, evaluate decisions, and improve them. This clearly communicates avoiding complete reliance on a third-party system.
